title: Non-Clifford Benchmarking via Ensemble Feature Selection
authors: Stancho G. Stanchev, Nikolay V. Vitanov
abstract: We propose an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) method for fast estimation of process infidelity of involutory multi-qubit gates, including non-Clifford targets, for which standard Clifford-based benchmarking does not apply. The method selects a compact set of experimentally executable circuit measurements from a candidate pool through offline training on a physically motivated ensemble of noisy channels, and combines them into a linear estimator with weights learned by ridge regression. The training ensemble is an explicit and tunable component of the protocol, incorporating prior knowledge about dominant hardware noise mechanisms. The estimator is validated on ibm_kingston using two Clifford validation benchmarks structurally related to the transpiled CCZ circuit, against independent Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB). Both show close EFS-IRB agreement across a wide range of process infidelities, with an estimation precision of approximately 0.01 over a process infidelity range of 0.02-0.2. EFS is subsequently applied directly to CCZ on the same device.
summary: The authors introduce Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS), a novel technique to estimate process infidelity for difficult non-Clifford quantum gates. By training on an ensemble of simulated noisy channels and using ridge regression, EFS constructs a robust linear estimator. Validation on superconducting hardware confirms that EFS provides accurate measurements comparable to established methods like IRB.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a reliable method to estimate process infidelity for multi-qubit gates, especially non-Clifford targets, where standard Clifford-based benchmarking techniques fail.
main_result: The proposed Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) method shows strong agreement with independent Randomized Benchmarking measurements on superconducting hardware, achieving high estimation precision across a wide range of gate infidelities.
method: EFS selects a compact set of executable circuit measurements from a candidate pool using offline training on a physically motivated ensemble of noisy channels and combines them into a linear estimator via ridge regression.
model_or_system: The work is validated on superconducting hardware (ibm_kingston) using three-qubit non-Clifford gates like CCZ. The analysis relies on Pauli Transfer Matrices to define process fidelity and infidelity ($\epsilon$).
key_observables: Process infidelity ($\epsilon$), gate fidelity ($F(G, T)$), and comparison metrics against independent Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking (IRB).
important_parameters: Estimation precision of $\approx 0.01$ over an infidelity range of $0.02-0.2$. The optimal feature set size was determined to be around $M=24$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a physically motivated training ensemble incorporating prior knowledge about dominant hardware noise mechanisms, and that the target gate satisfies an anchor condition.
figures_summary: Figures compare EFS estimates against true process infidelity from independent IRB measurements for Clifford benchmarks (ICCZ, CZ(0, 2)), demonstrating strong linear correlation. Further comparisons test transferability to non-Clifford gates like CCZ.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework using Pauli Transfer Matrices and an anchor condition, details the EFS methodology involving ensemble training and ridge regression, validates the estimator against independent IRB measurements on Clifford targets, and finally applies it directly to estimate infidelity for non-Clifford gates like CCZ.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial tool for characterizing noise in complex quantum hardware beyond simple gate sets, which is vital for scaling up quantum computation by providing reliable benchmarking metrics.

figures.caption: FIG. 2: Combined RMSE as a function of the number of selected features M for L ∈4, 8. The training ensemble contains noisy realizations of I, CZ(0, 2) and CCZ gener- ated with different random seeds. Consequently, a single EFS estimator is learned simultaneously for all three tar- gets, resulting in the same RMSE curve.

FIG. 1: Error decomposition of the training ensemble (K = 5000 realizations). Top left: (u, v) scatter separat- ing coherent (u) and incoherent (v) contributions. Top right: (a, c) scatter separating anticommuting (a) and commuting (c) parts relative to the involutory target. Bottom left: distribution of the sampled infidelity ε, bi- ased toward larger errors to improve training coverage. Bottom right: distribution of the coherent error angle θ.

FIG. 3: EFS estimates vs true process infidelity for CCZ (red) and CZ(0, 2) (blue) from Aer Simulator with inde- pendent test ensemble and SPAM/readout errors. Both targets yield slope ≈0.9–0.92, confirming that the esti- mator is equally applicable to non-Clifford gates.

FIG. 4: EFS vs IRB for ICCZ and CZ(0, 2) on ibm_kingston with M = 24. Fitted slopes and inter- cepts are very similar for the two targets (α = 0.94 and α = 0.93, both with intercept 0.012); combined r = 0.957, RMSEcal = 0.0099, over ε ≈0.02–0.20.

FIG. 5: EFS estimates for CCZ versus ICCZ on ibm_kingston across all valid qubit triples (α = 0.92, r = 0.925, RMSE = 0.0159). The close agreement for the large majority of triples confirms the expected domi- nance of diagonal noise; the few outliers (≈3–4%) reveal measurable non-diagonal error structure made detectable by the Rz(±π/4) redistribution.
